issues.headline: Better ground data. Better installation assurance.
issues.intro: This week’s developments highlight two parts of the monopile delivery chain: geotechnical information gathered before projects are built, and verification of foundation condition after installation. A new centrifuge dataset also offers useful evidence for cyclic pile–soil response in sand.
issues.takeaway: Can the project team connect site investigation, installation records and post-installation measurements into one traceable assessment? That evidence chain is essential when judging whether a more advanced soil model improves an actual installation decision.

items.title: Fugro secures a multi-year North Sea geotechnical investigation framework.
items.summary: On 5 November, Fugro announced a multi-year framework agreement with Germany’s Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) for geotechnical site investigations in the German North Sea. The scope includes offshore drilling, seabed cone penetration testing and laboratory testing. The programme is scheduled to begin in mid-March 2027, with data intended to support future wind-farm tendering and development.
items.implication: This is a useful signal that high-quality ground characterisation remains a core part of offshore-wind project de-risking. For monopile design and drivability, the value lies in linking CPT and laboratory evidence to representative stratigraphy, stress history and soil behaviour—not simply increasing the volume of investigation data.

source.name: Fugro · Official announcement
source.access_note: Official company announcement; scope and programme timing reported by Fugro.

items.title: Fugro to inspect all 64 monopile locations at East Anglia TWO.
items.summary: Fugro announced a post-installation seabed survey contract from Cadeler for the 960 MW East Anglia TWO offshore wind farm. From early 2027, a work-class remotely operated vehicle will inspect 64 monopile locations. The survey is intended to verify installation quality and provide information relevant to long-term foundation integrity.
items.implication: Post-installation verification is an important complement to drivability prediction. Installation models estimate how a foundation may behave during driving; seabed and foundation inspections help establish what was actually installed. Where available, measured installation and inspection records can provide valuable independent evidence for model assessment and future calibration.

source.name: Offshore Energy
source.access_note: Industry report dated 4 November 2026; project scope attributed to Fugro and Cadeler.

items.title: A new centrifuge dataset captures 23 cyclic monopile tests in dense sand.
items.summary: Wang, Askarinejad and Pisanò published an open-access Data in Brief article describing 23 geotechnical centrifuge tests: two monotonic and 21 cyclic tests on a model monopile in dense Geba sand at a target relative density of 80%. The tests were conducted at 100 g and provide measurements for examining monotonic and cyclic lateral pile response.
items.implication: A well-documented test matrix can support independent comparisons of cyclic soil–pile response, including loading-history effects. The dataset concerns dense silica sand and lateral loading; it should not be treated as direct validation of vibratory installation or carbonate-sand breakage modelling. Its value is as a complementary benchmark for cyclic foundation behaviour.

source.name: Data in Brief · Wang, Askarinejad and Pisanò
source.access_note: Open-access data article; online publication date 3 November 2026.

issues.headline: From port readiness to the behaviour of crushable sands.
issues.intro: Our opening edition follows a foundation delivery milestone in the Baltic and two research papers on calcareous-soil response. An Australian programme update provides context for the decisions these developments could inform.
issues.takeaway: A useful industry case should connect the soil response to a specific installation decision. The next question is which measurements would reduce uncertainty enough to change that decision.

items.title: BC-Wind receives its first monopiles in Poland.
items.summary: Ocean Winds reports that the first BC-Wind monopiles have arrived at Świnoujście Offshore Terminal. Local contractors are preparing the ground and supporting handling, transport and storage before the foundations move offshore. This is a delivery and logistics milestone; offshore installation is still to follow.
items.implication: Foundation delivery links port readiness, handling capacity and the installation campaign. For developers, this is a useful reminder to assess drivability uncertainty within the wider construction schedule, rather than as an isolated soil parameter.

items.title: A work-based breakage law for coral sand.
items.summary: Weijian Liu and co-authors combine monotonic and short-term cyclic testing with a generalised plasticity model for coral sand. Their formulation links relative breakage to plastic work and incorporates it into critical-state and dilatancy relations. The paper also describes joint parameter calibration using CMA-ES.
items.implication: This offers a relevant comparison for choosing calibration targets and examining how breakage changes soil response. It does not validate MONOPILE X or establish performance for a full-scale pile installation.

source.name: Ocean Engineering · Liu et al.
source.access_note: Based on publisher abstract and highlights; journal issue date shown.

items.title: Testing lateral response in calcareous sand.
items.summary: Yuteng Liu and co-authors compare monopiles and pile–bucket composite foundations in 1g model tests under monotonic and multistage cyclic lateral loading. The study examines how foundation configuration and loading history influence response in calcareous sand.
items.implication: The test programme is relevant to selecting lateral-response benchmarks and loading sequences. Its composite-foundation results should not be transferred directly to a standalone monopile or treated as evidence of vibratory installation savings.

source.name: Ocean Engineering · Liu et al.
source.access_note: Based on publisher abstract and highlights; journal issue date shown.

items.title: Deliverability remains central to Victoria’s offshore-wind programme.
items.summary: Offshore Wind Energy Victoria states that its first 2 GW auction opened in August 2026, with bids accepted until August 2027 and awards expected in 2028. Assessment includes value for money and deliverability. This is ongoing programme context, not an announcement from the past week.
items.implication: For geotechnical research, the useful connection is a traceable account of installation risk and the evidence needed to reduce it. Better predictions would need to demonstrate a decision benefit before any schedule or cost saving could be claimed.

source.name: Offshore Wind Energy Victoria
source.access_note: Current official programme page; date checked is shown.
